projectOutComesReport:
Project Outcomes 

From 2021-2023, this REU site project operated successfully throughout the award cycle at the University of North Texas (UNT) , focusing on interdisciplinary research experience in accelerated deep learning through a hardware-software collaborative approach. The REU program hosted 28 undergraduate students to engage in research projects during the summer. The students got motivated and mentored through various research projects so that they can make good preparations for pursuing advanced degrees and careers in STEM-related areas. The program offers a 10-week summer program to provide a hands-on research and educational experience to undergraduate students per year in the area of AI and machine learning with an emphasis on hardware-software co-design. 35% of the participants came from underrepresented groups such as women and Latinx communities. 39% of participants came from institutions with no graduate research programs related to AI. 6 students came from institutions without graduate programs in computer science. 53% of participants joined as freshman or sophomore students. Nearly all students had no previous experience engaging in research activities at their own institutions and had little knowledge of AI and machine learning. During the time of this award, program operations were continuously evaluated and updated in order to improve the research experience for the participants. By the time this award ends, all participants have gained valuable research experience in AI and machine learning and are on track to embark on successful careers in STEM.

Intellectual Merit

This REU project helped introduce AI and machine learning knowledge to undergraduate students who are eager to learn AI related technologies and want to pursue a career in this field. Students learned the concepts, models, programming tools and libraries, and the hardware systems that can accelerate the deep learning applications. This project provided students with opportunities to develop interdisciplinary skills for creating software models and evaluating their models using hardware accelerators. Each student was assigned to a team and trained by their mentor and graduate assistants to develop their own machine learning-based solution to the problems they are interested in, including image processing, DNA classification, environment protection, disease detection, particle identification in physics, etc. Students were guided through the research process of defining and characterizing a problem, developing novel solution and evaluating the results. This procedure involves one-on-one mentoring from faculty, technical support from graduate assistants and peer discussion. Participants improved their communication skills through presentations and learned how to write technical reports and papers. By the end of the REU program, this award resulted in 6 publications including accepted and submitted papers which are co-authored by 9 REU students in the program.

Broader Impacts

Recognizing the importance of AI and machine learning in reshaping the way problems are solved and the urge of students to master AI tools, this program was designed to provide students with an inter-disciplinary research experience in hardware-software co-design of deep neural networks.  The goal of this REU was to educate and empower participants to become the next generation researchers and engineers in AI. Professional development activities were designed  to motivate students to pursue STEM degrees and become better researchers. Technical trainings include designing models, learning software tools and libraries, and developing hardware accelerators with higher performance. Activities have also been developed to improve the skills of participants in scientific communication, leadership and technical writing. All students presented their work in a seminar at the end of each summer. By the end of this award, of the 16 participants who graduated from college, 5 students enrolled into graduate programs pursuing a master's or doctorate degree.

abstractText:
Fungi can synthesize small molecules with complex structures using a number of highly coordinated enzymes.  These molecules are difficult to make synthetically, and they can aid in crop production or have beneficial human health effects. This project will identify fungal enzymes that efficiently modify more than one substrate in a predictable way.  Also, enzymes will be engineered to expand the range of substrates. A biomanufacturing platform to synthesize bioactive molecules at lower costs will be the end result. In this project, students will be trained in core STEM technologies, with a focus on commercial applications.

Cytochalasans are phytotoxic, cytotoxic and actin-binding natural products. Produced by fungi, over 400 variants have been described. The structural diversity is partly explained by the flexibility of the enzymes that introduce and modify functional groups. These enzymes structurally rearrange the core carbon skeleton in a site-selective manner, often on more than one substrate. Genome mining will be used to identify cytochalasan tailoring enzymes. Overproducing strains will be characterized chemically. Transcription factor over-expression will be investigated.  Targeted gene knock-out will confirm the function and scope of the enzymes.  The enzymes will be engineered to expand their substrate range. Synthetic biology and metabolic engineering tools will be used to generate a biomanufacturing platform for large scale production and functionalization of cytochalasan-based carbon skeletons. This project will generate fundamental knowledge on how to effectively engineer enzymes and metabolic pathways for efficient and rapid structural diversification of bioactive molecules with commercial potential.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Cytochalasans are a large family of fungal secondary metabolites with a vast range of biological activities. Their major biological role appears to be inhibiting actin polymerization which is essential for cell structure and function. Despite the large number of unique cytochalasans reported (>500) very few are commerically available for in depth biological studies as most are discovered in individual research groups from private collections of fungi.

In this study we took a genome mining approach to identify commerically available fungi with the genetic potential to produce cytochalasans. We selected to work with Aspergillus heteromorphus & Aspergillus sclerotioniger, Colletotrichum spinosum & Colletotrichum sidae, Metarhizium brunneum and Metarhizium robertsii as well as the known cytochalasan producers Pyricularia grisea, Aspergillus clavatus, Chaetomium globosum, and the newly described Peroneutypa sp. M16 as they span multiple genera and it is unknown which biological signals induce cytochalasan production. 

We focused on understanding the site-selective and stereochemical considerations of cytochrome P450 monooxygenase (P450) enzymes that are essential for functionalizing cytochalasan backbones and altering biological activities. Rigorous bioinformatics work revealed that P450s can be sub-divided into P450s that functionalize the macrocycle moiety and those that functionalize the cyclohexene. Through in vitro studies with cytochalasans produced by P. sp M16 we could determine that the cyclohexene associated P450s are epoxidases and that epoxide opening is a spontaneous chemical reaction. Through combinatorial biosynthesis we investigated macrocycle P450s to determine how some of these enzymes perform iterative chemistry and discovered that the iterative nature of the enzyme is restricted depending on the structure of the macrocycle. Furthermore we established that despite these P450 enzymes being highly promiscuous in their native environments, they have extremely rigid stereochemical restrictions, indicating that the stereochemistry of carbons in the macrocycle is set by the PKS-NRPS responsible for their biosynthesis. This is important knowledge for synthetic chemists who may opt to use chemoenzymatic synthesis for introducing specific funtional groups. Finally, we established  the non-enzymatic incorporation of hydroxylamine into a natural product through isotopically labelled precursor feeding and in vitro studies.

In parallel training projects, we discovered several novel non-cytochalasan molecules, including unguisin J isolated from A. heteromorphus, and identified potential biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs). The discovery of a depside from C. spinosum  led us propose a structural revision for colletotric acid isolated from Colletotrichum sp. This information is populated into MiBIG a publicly accessible repository for natural product researchers that links BGCs and compound structure information. 

3 TAMS students, 1 undergraduate student, 4 PhD students, and 3 postdoctoral scholars participated in this study and were trained on relevants techniques that spanned multiple disciplines.  The three postdocs also had opportunities to train undergraduates and TAMs students either on this project or closely related projects running in parallel. Of the publications that have resulted, all have postdoc (co)-first authors and all have PhD student authors either as co-first (2) or second (2) authors, emphasizing their contributions. All participants had numerous opportunities to present their findings at regional and national conferences including: UNT Scholar's Day; BDI seminar, BDI EXPO; Fort Worth Regional Science and Engineering Fair, International Science and Engineering Fair, ESML summer school; John Innes Center summer school; American Society of Pharmacognosy annual meeting; ASP Student Chapter webinar; Gordon Research Conference on Enzymes, Co-enzymes, and Cofactors. To encourage and support students interested in interdisciplinary research, the Division of Chemical Biology was established and the graduate student curriculum is updated to include a course on Biosynthetic Chemistry.

abstractText:
This Faculty Early Career Development (CAREER) grant supports fundamental research to elucidate a new strategy of manufacturing nanoporous ceramic structures with controllable structure and composition and programmable mechanical stability. Nanoporous ceramic materials play a pivotal role in a broad range of emerging technologies, including sensing devices, water purification and filtration systems, and catalytic materials, which are important to national prosperity and welfare. Despite previous efforts on nanoscale patterning of inorganic materials, the limited accessibility to the available surfaces and interfaces remains a central problem in defining the functionality of the material systems. The ability to predict and control location-specific microstructures of materials and correlate this knowledge to their properties greatly extends current manufacturing capabilities for low-temperature processing of ceramics with high customizability, precision, and accuracy that are critically important for their potential use in engineering research and industrial applications. This research is complemented by offering new educational opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students in the areas of materials synthesis, mechanics, and surface science, with an emphasis on recruiting and retaining women and under-represented minorities for the next-generation manufacturing workforce. The projected outreach activities increase public awareness and readiness for advanced manufacturing capabilities and materials design concepts. 

The specific goal of this research is to discover processing-structure-property relationships in ceramic coatings and heterostructures by providing fundamental insights on the mechanism of liquid phase swelling-based infiltration of spin-coated polymer templates with inorganic precursors and defining the rules that control the resulting structure and, thus, access to various materials’ surfaces and interfaces. By in-situ monitoring of the swelling-induced evolution and infiltration of amphiphilic block copolymer templates using a quartz crystal microbalance and grazing-incidence small-angle x-ray scattering techniques, the study investigates the formation mechanisms of organic/inorganic surfaces and interfaces and unravels the guiding principles of ceramic material reconstruction. The structure knowledge that is thus revealed is correlated with the mechanical behavior of the coatings or films towards evaluating the influence of porosity on the stability of these materials and to quantify the damage tolerance of these structures under exposure to different environments and stresses. The accomplishment of the project objectives allows for creating a robust scalable manufacturing approach applicable to the large genome of nanoporous ceramics and other materials.

abstractText:
1706025 Ma

Recently, 20 million gallons of untreated wastewater were released into Florida's Tampa Bay during Hurricane Hermine, and 215 million gallons of slightly radioactive water entered the Floridian Aquifer through a sinkhole opening. In Florida, these events have caused considerable concern from local residents and state officials, as have similar events across the country. With the advent of a multitude of new materials, it may be time to examine the ways in which our water is treated and our ability to treat surge conditions. This project seeks to develop and deploy a new class of porous organic polymers which have high capacity and selectivity to rapidly remove heavy metal contaminants well below parts per million level standards set by the Environmental Protection Agency.

The project will engineer porosity and surface chemistry of porous organic polymers to clean inorganic heavy metal contaminants from both surface water and wastewater.  Porous organic polymers are robust, chemically and thermally stable, scalable, and modular, with very high surface area. The modularity of these polymers allows for a molecular-level tuning of the pore structure and surface chemistry that allows for engineered site-specificity of binding sites that target the heavy metal contaminants. Recent data shows these new materials offer a significant increase in capacity relative to benchmark materials, with a rapid removal of mercury and other heavy metal ions. This project will advance the concept by exploring rational design of these porous polymers with different topologies by customizing the monomer with various binding groups. The objectives of the project include design, synthesis, and characterization, followed by assessment of these materials to remove inorganic contaminants from water, and thirdly, development of materials with multiple recognition sites for removal of complex inorganic contaminants. The work will impact wastewater treatment, including municipal water, as well as the nuclear, fracking, and mining industries. The PIs will continue to mentor underrepresented groups in their laboratory and present a summer workshop and a web page regarding materials, energy, and the environment for first-generation college students.

projectOutComesReport:
This research project aimed to develop porous organic polymers (POPs) as a new class of adsorbent materials for water purification, which has been achieved through a series of proposed specific objectives including: (i) POP design, synthesis, and characterization; (ii) assessment for removing inorganic contaminants; and (iii) develop multivariate POPs featuring multiple recognition sites for simultaneous capture of multiple inorganic contaminants.

    During the entire period of the research project, a new approach via chemically engineering advanced porous materials at the atomic/molecular level using molecular building blocks that are environmentally stable has been developed for the removal of threatening water-based contaminants in surface water and waste-water streams.  A series of new POP materials that exhibit high porosity and a high density of binding sites with an affinity for contaminants have been prepared, which outcompete some benchmark materials for the removal of heavy metal ions, nuclear wastes, and micro-pollutants from water.  In addition, some new synthetic methodologies have been developed for the construction of POPs and other types of porous materials. Moreover, the insightful studies on the interactions between the contaminants and POP materials have provided some guidance for the design of new materials for water purification and other environmental remedies in the future.

  This research project has helped the PI to renew his commitment to the environment, and train future researchers and underrepresented groups how materials can help clean the environment. During the entire period of the project, 2 Ph.D. students, 2 undergraduate students, and 4 postdoctoral scholars have been well trained. The research project has contributed to the publication of 22 journal articles.

abstractText:
In recent years, governments have begun to connect parks and other large natural areas by conserving wildlife corridors – swaths of semi-natural land intended to allow the free flow of animals between natural areas. The hope is that the connected areas will sustain large, genetically diverse populations and ecological processes, such as pollination and seed dispersal. But there is little science to guide how wildlife corridors are put into practice and to minimize their costs, including costs of restricting human uses of the land. How many and what types of fences, roads, pastures, gardens, and buildings can be permitted in the corridor? How wide do corridors need to be?  Do some wildlife species use corridors more readily than others? Most of what we think we know about corridors comes from small experiments on 3-acre patches of habitat connected by 100-ft-wide corridors with no human activities nearby, and using animal presence or movement to measure corridor effectiveness. This study will involve corridors and patches 100 times larger, and in landscapes with various human activities nearby. Furthermore, this project will use genetics instead of animal presence or movement as a better way to measure how well corridors work. By these innovations and by measuring responses of multiple species, this study will help scientists understand corridor effectiveness. It will also help society implement corridors that are effective while minimizing all sorts of costs. 

This study will use large corridors and habitat patches that have been stable for 50-200 years, so that genetic patterns reflect the influence of landscape pattern. Each landscape contains a corridor connecting two natural patches and two types of reference conditions, namely two patches lacking a connection that are about the same size and interpatch distance as the connected patches, and an intact natural area containing two sampling locales with similar size and spacing. The study will use 20 independent landscapes to quantify how corridor traits affect gene flow, and will use non-flying mammals as focal species because they are strongly affected by fragmentation. The research team hypothesizes (1) a strong non-linear decline in success (gene flow) with corridor length, reflecting the skewed distribution of dispersal distances within species; (2) success will drop steeply as corridor width falls below a threshold, with the threshold determined by species traits; and (3) species that are bigger, are habitat specialists, or have greater dispersal abilities (relative to brain size or reproductive rate) will benefit more from corridors. Testing these hypotheses will allow generalization to a wide range of mammal species not included in this project. We will use highly flexible Random Forest models to answer the overarching question: What landscape traits (e.g., corridor width, degree of human disturbance) and species traits (mobility, affinity to particular land cover types) are associated with effective corridors?

Intellectual Merit and Project Background:

Conservation corridors are the most frequently cited intervention available to land managers and conservationists to protect and preserve biodiversity in light of ongoing human land use and climate destabilization. However, their potential usefulness at protect biodiversity is often based on theory or from data derived from model ecosystems. These studies all utilized simplifying assumptions to investigate corridor potential, and generally found that corridors work. However, studies of actual landscapes indicated that corridor functionality was more equivocal, with some working, some failing, and some having little to no impact. Despite mixed scientific evidence, governments spend tens of millions of dollars annually on conservation corridors. Our research seeks to identify factors associated with corridos that actually preserve biodiversity and which features make them successful. The goal of our research was to curate a set of data on real-world corridors and quantify the degree to which they facilitated biodiversity by promoting dispersal (gene flow). This information will be useful to practitioners and managers as they continue to develop corridors, by providing scientific backing that such investments are likely to provide the intended benefits.

We studied 29 real-world corridors, on 13 landscapes, across 3 continents. Corridors ranged in length from 500m to 71km and widths from 100m to 1.5km wide. Each corridor was embedded in a highly human modified landscape context with a range of human activities occurring within. Our analysis includes genetic diversity, gene flow, and patch occupancy data for 14 mammal species (small mammals, meso-carnivores, and carnivores) dependent on the natural vegetation for their natural history dispersal. In addition to corridors, each of our study landscapes contained a large intact reference area, and isolated patches to act as reference conditions (Figure 1).

Key Outcomes:

Over the course of six years, we curated a dataset that included 2,803 unique samples/genotypes from 14 species at an average of 11.63 loci/species.  We also collected a suite of site-specific landscape attribute data from each of the sampled landscapes including: corridor width, corridor length, corridor tortuosity, number of roads and linear barriers crossing the corridor, and management within the corridor. We used this data set to test three questions related to conservation corridor functionality:

  1. Does the presence of a corridor between two sample areas promote gene flow of the focal species? 
  2. What, if any, attributes of the corridor promote higher levels of gene flow among focal species?
  3. Does the presence of a corridor promote higher genetic diversity and reduced inbreeding among focal species?

Using a combination of Random Forest Analysis and a perMANOVA we were able to draw the following conclusions about corridor efficacy. 

  • Corridors work - they increase genetic connectivity by up to 64%: The presence of a corridor connecting sample locations was the single best predictor of gene flow. Removing the presence of corridors reduced model performance predicting gene flow by up to 64%. This strongly suggests that corridors provide increased connectivity for focal species across a range of species and landscape traits.
  • Keep them straight - winding corridors are less effective: Corridor tortuosity (how winding or curved a corridor is) was the single best explanatory variable as to why corridors increased gene flow among connected patches. In general, gene flow among connected patches remained high until tortuosity exceeded 1.2. We also observed that landscape management within the corridor was also important.
  • Corridors facilitate movement more than increase local genetic diversity: Results from the perMANOVA suggested that there was little evidence that the presence of the corridor increased genetic diversity, effective population size, or reduced inbreeding among focal species. 

These results strongly suggest that that conservation corridors are beneficial to conserve biodiversity in light of current land use and climate destabilization. These benefits occur on long or short corridors embedded in human dominated landscapes. However, corridors should be as simple as possible, with straight direct conduits providing greater likelihood of success. Our results also highlight a reason for the apparent discrepancies between the high success of experimental corridors compared to the more complex patterns observed in real-world systems. Experimental corridors typically simplify the landscape to contain a straight corridor of more or less uniform natural vegetation. Our results suggest that these are nearly the perfect corridor to ensure success. The degree to which real-world corridors deviate in shape and internal land use heterogeneity may lower the likelihood of corridor success.

Broader Impact:

These results will provide the basis for future corridor design and management plans and enable the development of successful corridors. Our data demonstrate corridors are potentially beneficial to biodiversity conservation when designed, implemented, and managed correctly. In addition, we have hosted an international workshop to train 24 post docs, graduate, and undergraduate researchers in spatial analysis techniques. This project also contributed to the training of 3 MS, 1 PhD student, and numerous undergraduate students

abstractText:
Powerful and ubiquitous sensors and devices nowadays can collect data on all types of human activities and natural phenomena. These data sets are usually aggregated and stored in a distributed storage system, from which information can then be retrieved as needed for processing and computation. Making such systems private and secure is of paramount importance, which has motivated the study of private information retrieval (PIR) systems, which can provide strong privacy guarantees on the access to information in these databases. Characterizing the level of guarantees will help assess the usefulness of a PIR system. This project aims to develop a holistic information theoretic view of PIR systems, which can provide important theoretical guidance on the design of private, secure, and efficient information retrieval systems.
 
In the framework of this holistic view, this project seeks to identify the information theoretic limits and develop efficient code constructions for the optimal tradeoffs between important system constraints, including communication, storage, complexity, and security. This holistic view goes beyond many information theoretic studies that focus on a single aspect of the system constraints, namely the communication cost. The project is expected to significantly advance the state-of-the-art: it seeks to provide a better balanced and comprehensive understanding on the tradeoffs between different constraints in general information retrieval systems.

projectOutComesReport:
This project develops a holistic view of private information retrieval systems where data is collected in a distributed manner while the privacy of user behavior is protected, using information theory tools. Theoretical guarantees are derived for various performance metrics of such distributed systems, including communication rate (how much data needs to be downloaded for desired information retrieval), storage cost (how much data needs to be stored at distributed storage nodes), computational complexity (how much computation needs to be performed for retrieval), and security and privacy levels (how much undesired information can be revealed and how much collusion may be tolerated) and the tradeoff among the metrics.

New problems are formulated that include a storage code design problem which allows and turns out to necessite non-linear codes (rare in the literature), a problem with multiple levels of privacy where files with different importance level may tolerate different number of colluding servers, and a multi-user retrieval problem which allows users with distinct storage capabilities to simultaneously access data privately and jointly use the communication resource. New solutions are found that generalize traditional random coding and binning tools from classical information theory, introduce new alignment linear structures to recursive private retrieval protocols, symmetry guided and forced code constructions, tree structure based lower bounding analysis, reveal connection to other significant problems in security and privacy. A more comprehensive and balanced understanding of the fundamental limits of the tradeoff between the diverse array of performance metrics is obtained in general information retrieval systems.

Results from this project have been published as IEEE journal articles and have been presented at conference talks, including two tutorials, one at 2021 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory and one at 2024 IEEE International Conference on Communications, for broad audience in the general field of information theory and communications. Three Ph.D. graduate students participated in the research at various stages of this project and gained experience in information theory and coding research. Education materials produced from this project have been discussed in graduate level information theory and seminar classes.

abstractText:
Cooperative perception enables vehicles to exchange sensor data among each other to achieve collaborative object detection and classification, which is extremely useful to enhance autonomous vehicles' safety as they frequently suffer from blind spots and/or occlusions. Without proper measures in place for data protection, however, very few vehicles are likely to share their sensor data, due to the concerns on potential privacy leakage. A vehicle can encrypt its sensor data before sharing it with others, however, data encryption only protects data security during transmission, i.e., a receiving vehicle can still access private and sensitive information after it decrypts the data. To address this issue, a privacy-preserving convolutional neural network (CNN) is designed so that encrypted sensor data generated by vehicles can be fused and processed to produce ciphertext-based object detection results. Although a receiving vehicle obtains meaningful object detection results from received ciphertexts, it has no means to recover the original data, thus protecting the privacy of data shared from other vehicles. The proposed technique is a generic solution that can be extended to offer data privacy protection for other machine learning methods. This project will be transformative because it will enable vehicles to securely share useful sensor data between each other. Such an advance can be extremely beneficial for extending the line of sight and field of view of autonomous vehicles, which secures the public safety and advances smart transportation and national prosperity. This project offers a wide variety of research activities, ranging from CNN analysis, security algorithm design, and hardware programming. The investigators will actively engage students with various backgrounds in this project. Special efforts will be made to increase the participation of underrepresented student researchers. A workshop on Connected and Autonomous Vehicles will be organized annually to promote the research outcomes from this project to the industry and research communities and benefit society.

The goal of this project is to understand the security and privacy challenges in achieving cooperative perception among autonomous vehicles, and then design an effective and efficient privacy-preserving CNN for processing encrypted sensor data, shared from multiple vehicles. Leveraging the additive secret sharing technique, sensor data is first randomly split and encrypted into two ciphertexts, and then processed in the encrypted format by two non-colluding edge servers. To process the encrypted data, edge servers make use of a privacy-preserving CNN model that securely implements all layers in the original CNN, including the secure convolutional layer, secure activation layer, secure pooling layer, secure region proposal network layer, and secure full-connection layer. As an edge server possesses only a partial view of the sensor data, sensitive information contained in the data is protected. To optimize the privacy-preserving CNN model, cross-layer optimization and field programmable gate arrays (FPGA)-based acceleration techniques are designed to increase the speed of object detection and classification while keeping the energy consumption low. The proposed system will serve as a convincing proof-of-concept for data privacy protection using CNNs, thus opening the door to widespread adoption of privacy-preserving CNN in processing sensor data. The source code and the privacy-preserving CNN model, along with its training and testing datasets, will be made publicly available, serving as a catalyst for enabling innovative research on data privacy protection in vehicular edge systems.

projectOutComesReport:
We developed an innovative privacy-preserving data-sharing framework for cooperative perception on connected self-driving cars. In this framework, a vehicle can choose specific objects (e.g., pedestrain or license plate number) to keep confidential before sharing datawith other vehicles. By harnessing the exceptional performance of existing models in image segmentation and inpainting tasks, a vehicle can easily identify sensitive objects within its collected sensor data and construct inpainted images after the sensitive objects are removed.These privacy preserving inpainted images are then securely transmitted to receivers, facilitating privacy preserved data sharing among vehicles and between vechicles and roadside servers.Experiments reveal that our solution is quick and efficient, achieving secure segmentation in just 3.47 seconds and secure inpainting in 0.99 seconds. Notably, the results from our method match those from the original deep neural networks, ensuring that data privacy is preserved.


As the secure fuctions implemented in our solution are based on the deep neural network technology, the number of parameters and computations are large, which puts aheavy burden on the underlying computing platforms and runtime systems. To enhance inference speed, we use quantization technique to enhance performance, reduce energy consumption, and, in most cases, maintain or improve accuracy when compared to existing deep neural network solutions. Our approach stands out, demonstrating a remarkable 67.6% improvement in performance speed and a significant 66.9% reduction in energy consumption, with minimal accuracy loss (less than 0.6%) compared to traditional quantization methods.


This project has trained four Ph.D. students (including two females), six undergraduate students, and two high school students. Six undergraduate students received ten-week traing through the NSF Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU) at University of North Texas (UNT). They learned how to conduct research, including problem identification and formulation, literature review, brainstorming ideas, group discussion, scientific writing, peer-reviewing, and research presentation. Two high school students were trained on this project through the Texas Academy of Mathematics and Science (TAMS) program offered at the UNT. These students were able to make a poster presentation at UNT’s Scholars Day, 2022. One female Ph.D. student successfully defended her dissertation on deep neural network acceleration in 2022. A new course on "Connected and Autonomous Vehicle System" was designed and offered at UNT. It is a graduate-level research-oriented course for the connected and autonomous vehicles. The main objective of the course is to help students understand the research challenges on computing, and communication, security, and privacy, in connected and autonomous vehicle systems. Last but not the least, we've contributed to the academic community with a publication of ten peer-reviewed journal or conference papers resulting from this project.

abstractText:
ABSTRACT
 This award supports a research project that focuses on developing tools and best practices for promoting effective collaboration between legal and policy experts and roboticists. This collaboration serves two purposes: (1) to better ensure the safe and effective development of collaborative robots; and (2) to create effective and appropriate laws and policies governing their deployment in public spaces. The research team plans to develop a specification language and interactive tools for enabling reasoning about how robots and autonomous systems work, at a non-technical level. Combined with “What If?” case studies, this will facilitate dialog between technical experts and their legal and policy counterparts. The specification language and reasoning toolkit will be designed to evolve simultaneously with, and support, rapid changes in specific technology within the context of existing legal and policy frameworks. The team will use the legal concept of case studies to ground reasoning within a specific scenario. Each case study will consist of a complete description of how the necessary robot capabilities might be implemented, complete with assumptions and potential failures. The results of this research will enable legal and policy experts and roboticists to more accurately reason about the intersection of robotic systems and legal and policy frameworks before either are implemented. Specifically, this will support legal and policy experts in more accurately designing effective policy, legislation, and regulation around robotics that is meaningful and feasible, and will support robotic researchers in designing systems that incorporate legal and ethical questions into their design choices.

The research team will engage in an interdisciplinary development of a structured language paradigm (comprised of syntax, semantics, and system descriptions) that supports grounded reasoning about robotics in law and policy contexts. These language paradigms will be instantiated as interactive experiences that enable embodied reasoning and metaphor exploration by experts and non-experts alike. These experiences will be developed around a specific set of near-term, feasible robot tasks, existing robot capabilities and known failure modes, metaphors to explain those capabilities, and specific scenarios that highlight common misconceptions. These experiences will be evaluated on their effectiveness in enabling non-technical people to reason about, and predict, autonomous system behavior. On the legal and policy side, the research team will engage with experts in these areas to develop specific hypothetical case studies (based on the identified tasks) that illustrate how to view technological choices through a law and policy lens. Specifically, team members will work collaboratively to develop a set of associated design patterns that assist in mapping technical concepts to the structured language and the interactive visualizations, develop a prototype suite of interactive training applications, and construct a set of case studies for specific robot-use scenarios that enables meaningful dialog around law and policy and robotics.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The overarching goal of this collaborative research project between Oregon State University, Rhodes College and University of North Texas is to  improve law and policy development for  robotics. Our approach develops and evaluates the use of exploratory experiences, and it leverages users' knowledge of common applications based on computer vision and other technologies incorporated into robotic systems (e.g. mapping, video-teleconferencing, or translation of languages from images), to enhance reasoning about what robots can (and cannot) do, and how they are likely to fail.  One outcome of this work is the development of a Predict-Reason-Fix measure to assess a participant’s ability to reason about robotic capabilities and potential failures. We focus on sidewalk robots in a series of exploratory experiences and additional analyses because their task is easily explainable, not very high risk, and there are available existing use scenarios.

Our primary finding is that people are very good at reasoning about failures in applications that use computer vision and path planning (traditional robot tasks). By linking the technology in these applications to robotics, and thus leveraging experiential knowledge, people are better able to predict when a robot might succeed (or fail) at a task. Similarly, if people see example videos of real robots failing at a task, they are less likely to assume a robot is more capable than it is.

Additional outcomes of this research include multiple publications and presentations in both law-based and robotics conferences and professional venues, the development of embodied robotic reasoning experiences, and unique studies of sidewalk robots “in the wild.”  We have presented at multiple law-based events (including We Robot and the Oregon State Bar association), as well as participated in multiple panel discussions both nationally and internationally. As part of these events we devised several “pretend to be a robot” embodied reasoning experiences  that have people take on the role of different parts of the robot (camera, brains, arms). Running these experiences before the formal discussion sessions, at conferences such as We Robot, was helpful for non-technical people to reason better about actual (and not abstract) technologies the law might encounter. We also contributed to a white paper produced by the British Columbia Law Institute on AI and tort law. This white paper provides guidance on how tort law should deal with products that have an AI component. We produced an on-line game that walks participants through a sidewalk robot scenario, asking them to both develop a robot and outline policy around that robot. One team develops the robot, the other team is the “community”. The game requires participants to argue for (or against) specific robotic technologies and city policies based on their core values. We presented the game in several iterations at law-based events such as We Robot. We also conducted a unique set of studies of sidewalk robots. Oregon State University has had sidewalk robots (Starship) for food delivery for several years. We took advantage of this to do the first-ever set of studies of robots “in the wild” and how the campus community perceived these robots. Although perceptions were largely positive, the study brought up multiple access issues, including robots blocking intersections and crowding sidewalks, that need to be addressed.

abstractText:
This Grant for Rapid Response Research (RAPID) project will study emergency mangers’ and households’ evacuation decisions and their sheltering considerations during Hurricane Laura as individuals cope with the COVID-19 pandemic. It is important for the scientific community, policymakers, and emergency managers to understand how the simultaneous threats of a hurricane and a pandemic affect individual and household decisions about protecting themselves during these events. The findings from this project will help emergency managers and policymakers develop appropriate public health and population protection strategies to help communities be prepared for future events. With a better understating of the determinants of hurricane and pandemic protective actions (e.g. evacuation, social distancing, sheltering) compliance, emergency managers can develop better evacuation plans and warning messages to help reduce the impact of both the pandemic and hurricane, as well as to advance national health and welfare. More specifically, the scientific progress generated by this research will increase understanding of differences between emergency mangers’ and citizens’ concerns regarding the maintenance of shelters, sheltering locations (public shelters, hotels, friends’, and relatives’ house), evacuation routing, and evacuation modeling during a pandemic. Emergency managers will be able to better design and locate shelters and encourage households to take appropriate protective actions in the future when facing similar threats.
 
This project will advance the state of science about households’ and emergency mangers’ protective action decision-making processes by using a sequential mixed methods design. This study will use survey and interview methodologies to collect both quantitative and qualitative data from emergency managers and households in the Hurricane Laura risk areas in Texas and Louisiana. Because of the complexity of the event, this project requires the integration of variables in both the Protection Motivation Theory and the Protective Action Decision Model. The results of this study will build a new theoretical model that captures individuals’ protective action decision-making process in a dual hazard environment (hurricane and pandemic). This project will contribute to emerging research on pandemics and disasters in the United States, but with a focus on how the pandemic is shaping protective action decision-making, which has generalizability to other compound events.

projectOutComesReport:
This Rapid Response Research (RAPID) project investigates the evacuation decisions of emergency managers and households, along with their considerations for sheltering during Hurricane Laura, as individuals coped with the COVID-19 pandemic. It is crucial for the scientific community, policymakers, and emergency managers to understand how the concurrent threats of a hurricane and a pandemic impact individual and household protective action decisions during these events.

Intellectual merit: This research addresses a gap in the hazard risk perception literature by examining the associations among different aspects of threat perception and their effects on evacuation decisions. The findings contributed to risk theories that could be used for future situations where an environmental hazard is intertwined with respiratory infectious disease risk. Evacuation is an important protective action choice before, during, and after disasters such as hurricanes, floods, tsunamis, or wildfires. Project findings can be applied to ongoing and future studies focused on developing programs that facilitate a more efficient evacuation decision process. Additionally, the confluence of Hurricane Laura and COVID-19 posed a novel challenge for emergency management stakeholders. This study attempts to understand how COVID-19 affected emergency management operations in response to a familiar hazard. In general, evidence of improvisation was found during the planning process among key stakeholders for hurricane season, the evacuation effort, and the sheltering operations in both Texas and Louisiana. Participants described a system that operated on inertia, adhering to normal hurricane planning and response operations until outside forces necessitated a change. Improvisation in the planning process in response to COVID-19 precautions and improvisation in the hurricane response was tied to attempts to address a last-minute shift to non-congregate sheltering imposed by their respective states. This improvisation led to varying approaches across the states in the evacuation effort, and each state encountered several challenges in managing the distributed evacuation effort remotely. Given the continued threat posed by COVID-19 and other respiratory illnesses, this study provides insights that emergency management stakeholders could apply to current and future planning and response efforts for hazards requiring evacuation and sheltering.

Broader Impact: The findings from this project can help emergency managers and policymakers develop appropriate public health and population protection strategies to prepare communities for future events. With a better understanding of the determinants of hurricane and pandemic protective actions compliance (e.g., evacuation, social distancing, sheltering), emergency managers can develop better evacuation plans and warning messages to reduce the impact of both the pandemic and hurricanes, as well as to advance national health and welfare. Specifically, the scientific progress generated by this research will increase understanding of the differences between emergency managers' and citizens' concerns regarding the maintenance of shelters, sheltering locations, evacuation routing, and evacuation modeling during a pandemic. Emergency managers will be better able to design and locate shelters and encourage households to take appropriate protective actions in the future when facing similar threats. Furthermore, the project's data is currently accessible upon request and will be deposited in an open-source data repository, DesignSafe-CI, within a year after the project concludes. The project findings have been successfully published in two major peer-review journals in the field of risk research and a technical report was published by the Natural Hazard Center. In addition, we delivered six conference presentations during the grant period. The materials used for data collection are employed in all the investigators' universities for a range of courses, including Introduction to Emergency Management and Disaster Science, Research Methods, Risk Analysis, etc. Additionally, the project has supported minority and female students pursuing their Masters and Ph.D. degrees.

abstractText:
Professor Thomas R. Cundari of the University of North Texas is supported by an award from the Chemical Catalysis program in the Division of  Chemistry to computationally study novel catalytic methods for upgrading light alkanes (e.g., methane or natural gas, ethane, etc.) to more valuable commodity chemicals and fuels (e.g. gasoline).  The conversion of light alkanes to more valuable products generally requires the use of metal-containing catalysts to speed up their conversion to specific desirable products.  Professor Cundari's students pursue novel routes for conversion of this abundant domestic energy resource that do not require dangerous, harsh or expensive chemical catalysts. The results of advanced computer simulations of methane reactions are integrated with the research of experimental collaborators to identify promising catalysts for this important chemical transformation. The large data sets generated by Cundari Group students are integrated with emerging machine learning techniques to identify novel chemical entities for methane conversion.  Early-career scientists engaged in this research gain experience in cutting-edge research with significant theory-experiment interplay in an area with obvious societal benefit.

Professor Thomas R. Cundari of the University of North Texas is supported by an award from the Chemical Catalysis program in the Division of Chemistry to investigate the fundamental importance of acid and base properties of alkane C-H bonds and metal-ligand active sites, respectively. Activation and functionalization of aliphatic C-H bonds is an important challenge in commodity and fine chemical synthesis, for homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts. Cundari Group students employ quantum mechanical and machine learning modeling to discern the extent of catalytic functionalization without using super-acid/-base reagents. Simulations by the Cundari Group are closely integrated with experiment and are further valuable chemistry community by establishing benchmarks for accuracy and precision of important catalytic and chemical properties.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The main emphases of grant CHE-1953547 involve the study of the fundamental acid-base properties of chemical entities and to decipher how these properties (a) can be manipulated by modification of the chemical environment, and (b) inform the reactivity of these entities for important catalytic transformations. Student researchers - graduate and undergraduate - focused on the used of advanced computer simulations of the chemistry of methane - the primary component of natural gas - and dinitrogen - the main constituent of air. They sought through this fundamental chemical research to understand how these abundant compounds may be economically converted to useful industrial products such as methanol (in the case of methane) and ammonia (in the case of dinitrogen). Our student research team demonstrated for the first time that there is a direct correlation between the reactivity of methane and the extent to which the acid-base properties are modulated. More importantly, significant changes in the rate of the chemical reactions not need necessarily engender large changes in the underlying chemical nature of methane. Similar conclusions were reached for dinitrogen. Likewise, we developed and implemented a similar computational strategy to understand how the chemical reactivity of the catalyst materials that react woth methane and nitrogen could be modified for greater activity. In terms of workforce development in the STEM arena, the research supported by the NSF through grant CHE-1953547 constitutes the first exposure of many of the junior scientists involved - who perform the majority of day-to-day scientific work - to the research endeavor. As such, essential skills in data entry and analysis, critical thinking, ideation and research collaboration are instilled in them, which serves them in their future career endeavors. Skills in scientific communication - both written and oral - are refined through the publication of scientific papers in quality, refereed journals and talks at local, regional and international chemical society meetings. Furthermore, a hallmark of training in our group - which focuses on cutting edge simulations and modeling - is its close collaboration with leading experimental groups. As such, our student team members not only receive important technical training, but get to develop their collaboration skills. Overall, more than a dozen junior scientists participated in research under the aegis of CHEM-19543547.

abstractText:
This collaborative research project, involving Michigan State University, the University of North Texas and the University of Michigan, will examine whether epistemic exclusion, a form a scholarly devaluation, may create a barrier to the full inclusion and participation of women and faculty of color in STEM. Epistemic exclusion is the devaluation of certain types of scholarship that occurs when invisible biases in systems of evaluation are coupled with prejudice toward, and negative stereotypes about, historically underrepresented groups.  Because faculty members' career outcomes (e.g., promotion, tenure, and turnover intentions) are determined by how well they meet evaluative standards, bias in systems of evaluation that disproportionately harm women and faculty of color may impede their retention and advancement in academia. The project team will create and validate a scale assessing faculty epistemic exclusion. 

Results of the project have the potential to benefit society by providing a tool that researchers can use to investigate epistemic exclusion in STEM faculty.  Advancing this line of research may result in potential interventions and policy changes at institutions of higher education that improve the retention and promotion of women and underrepresented minority STEM faculty at our nation’s colleges and universities.  There is a plan for dissemination to scholarly audiences through peer-reviewed presentation and publications in professional journals that will help inform the research and academic communities.  

This project is supported by the EHR Core Research (ECR) program, which supports work that advances fundamental research on STEM learning and learning environments, broadening participation in STEM, and STEM workforce development. The ECR program supports the accumulation of robust evidence to inform efforts to understand, build theory to explain, and suggest intervention and innovations to address persistent challenges in STEM interest, education, learning and participation.  The project was co-funded by the NSF ADVANCE program which supports the implementation of organizational change strategies to address systemic inequities that impact women in STEM faculty careers.  The project was also funded by the Alliances for Graduate Education and Professoriate (AGEP) program, which funds projects designed to advance knowledge about increasing the number of African Americans, Hispanic Americans, Native American Indians, Native Hawaiians and Native Pacific Islanders in STEM faculty careers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

abstractText:
With this award, the Chemical Catalysis Program is funding Dr. Hong Wang of the University of North Texas to develop new catalytic methods to synthesize chiral molecules. Chiral molecules exist as non-superimposable mirror images, the same difference as left and right hands. Many molecules, especially naturally-occurring organic compounds and many pharmaceuticals, are chiral and the two mirror image forms of the molecule often have different biological properties. Therefore, an important challenge in modern organic synthesis is to control the handedness of the product.  The reactions being developed in this project are designed to provide concise and versatile synthetic pathways to construct 5- and 7-membered ring systems, with control of handedness, a difficult feat with currently available synthetic methods. Dr. Wang is actively engaged in joint efforts to attract a diverse group of students to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields.  Her outreach activities build upon her research and includes outreach summer research programs for undergraduate students from minority schools and high school students to establish interest in STEM fields at an early stage.  

Dr. Hong Wang and her research team are developing novel catalytic systems through merging enamine catalysis with hard metal Lewis acid catalysis. The feasibility of the reversed soft-hard strategy is investigated to solve the critical acid-base quenching problem involved in cooperative acid-base catalysis. Also, under investigation is which factors affect the formation of enamine from primary arylamines and ketones. [3+2] and [4+3] reactions are developed using cooperative enamine-hard metal Lewis acid catalysis to construct 5- and 7-membered ring systems. In addition, a new class of bimetallic complexes is explored to serve as chiral hard metal Lewis acid catalysts in asymmetric catalysis. The density functional theory (DFT) calculations are carried out to understand the structure-activity of these bimetallic catalysts and the mechanisms of the [3+2] and [4+3] reactions. To address the broader impacts of this project, Dr. Wang is actively engaged in initiating outreach programs to provide summer research opportunities to undergraduate and high school students with a focus on attracting female and minority students into STEM fields.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
This project aims to develop novel catalytic systems for asymmetric organic transformations with particular focus on developing strategies to combine enamine catalysis with hard metal Lewis’s acid catalysis. New strategies including competition coordination and reversed soft-hard concept have been developed to resolve the challenging acid-base quenching problem in catalytic activation. Using these strategies, a range of readily accessible and atom-economy [3+3], [3+2] and [4+2] cycloaddition reactions have been developed to afford pyrrolidine, tetrahydroindoles, chromans, oxadiazinanes, benzofuran and indoles, which are important structural motifs present in a large variety of pharmaceuticals and biologically active natural products. Enamine formation from primary arylamines and cyclic ketones has been proved for the first time using NMR spectroscopy. This project has also introduced novel chiral bimetallic systems derived from phosphoric acids, which is expected to expand the toolbox for asymmetric catalysis. In addition, arylamine-based enamines radicals have also been uncovered, which are expected to enable new activation modes for constructing new C-C and C-heteroatom bond forming reactions.

This project has provided research opportunities to seven undergraduate students from University of North Texas, University of Texas and Westminster College. The training and research experience received by the students in this project have helped them gain admissions to chemistry graduate schools and find jobs in industry.

abstractText:
Human morphology varies widely around the world, but claims that adaptive benefits of certain physical features contribute to this variation have rarely been experimentally tested. This research will evaluate how differences in head, trunk, and limb anatomy influence the ability of individuals to regulate their internal body temperature when exposed to different environmental conditions, thereby, experimentally testing long-held assumptions regarding patterning of human body form. The investigators will share the results of this project through publications, STEM outreach activities, public talks, and interviews on a nationally recognized podcast. Graduate, undergraduate, and medical students will be trained in data collection and analysis, and field trip demonstrations of the project equipment and methods will be used to expose economically disadvantaged Texas high school students to potential careers in science and medicine. This project will also produce high-quality, whole body CT scans which will be made readily available to other researchers through an online data archive. Finally, this research will shed light on issues important to both the broader scientific community and the general public, including the significance of human biological diversity and the potential implications of global environmental change.

This research will experimentally test proposed relationships between thermoregulatory benefits and environmentally patterned variation in human anatomy. While climatic pressures are widely cited as contributing to global variation in human head shape, torso dimensions, limb proportions, and overall body size, specific links between physical features and body function in different environmental conditions have not been experimentally established. Furthermore, studies of adaptation to climate have historically focused on separate regions of the body (e.g. braincase, nose, torso, upper limb, lower limb), with minimal attention to how these different anatomical structures interact with one another to function as a whole. To remedy this, the research uses state-of-the-art technologies, including computed tomography imaging and an environmental chamber simulating different climactic conditions, to measure the physiological responses of physically diverse living participants. Validation of proposed thermoregulatory benefits of specific body forms is essential for guiding future research on adaptation. Further, by employing a whole-body approach, this study will clarify the role of different anatomical regions in overall thermoregulatory function. In sum, this study will explicitly link hard and soft tissue morphology to physiological outcomes, permitting more confident assessment of environmental adaptation in both modern populations and the fossil record.

abstractText:
The Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms plus the Axiom of Choice (ZFC) have been widely accepted as a foundation for mathematics; virtually all branches of mathematics that have been studied and applied to other scientific fields can be interpreted in ZFC. However, it turns out that there are natural and important mathematical theories which cannot be decided by ZFC alone. The Large Cardinal Axioms (LCAs) are extensions of ZFC designed to settle all such theories. This is Gödel's program in Set Theory. If an LCA is "correct," then the theories it decides are also correct. How can one test for correctness of an LCA? The Inner Model Program, a major program in modern Set Theory, justifies correctness by constructing canonical models for LCAs much like the natural numbers are the canonical model for the Peano Axioms of Arithmetic (PA) (and as such PA is a correct theory). This project contributes to the Inner Model Program by advancing methods for constructing canonical models for LCAs from various extensions of ZFC. The educational component includes annual conferences, curriculum development, and outreach and broadening participation activities. 

The project fits into the general framework of studying the connections between inner models, sets of reals, hybrid structures (such as hereditarily ordinal definable sets (HOD) of determinacy models), forcing, and strong combinatorial principles (such as the Proper Forcing Axiom (PFA)). The problem of building a canonical inner model for an LCA is referred to as the Inner Model Problem for that LCA. One of the project's main goals is to identify certain obstructions that may prevent the current approaches to resolving the Inner Model Problem for various LCAs from going further as well as proposing ways of overcoming them. Specifically, the project will study obstacles to the current techniques of the Core Model Induction (one such obstacle is the Sealing of the Universally Baire Sets) and develop new approaches to the Core Model Induction that overcome these obstacles. One main application of the above analyses is in constructing canonical inner models of large cardinals from various strong extensions of ZFC, like the Proper Forcing Axiom.

abstractText:
In recent years, researchers have applied artificial intelligence (AI) to effectively solve important problems in cybersecurity. While significant research progress has been made in cybersecurity with the help of AI, there is a shortage of highly educated workers who can solve challenging problems at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity. This project will develop such a workforce by educating qualified individuals from diverse communities in cybersecurity and AI simultaneously. The project team will develop and deliver modular and project-based courses for graduate students that cover the basics of  AI and cybersecurity using real-life problems. The development of innovative courses is intended to strengthen the student experience and to build a strong and diverse workforce in AI and cybersecurity that will fill the current voids in government, industry, and academia.

The project team will develop five modular courses for graduate students: (1) Scalable Advanced Analytics, (2) AI including Explainable Machine Learning (ML), (3) ML for Cybersecurity, (4) Cybersecurity for ML (e.g., Adversarial ML), and (5) Secure Blockchain Technologies. The design of these modular and hybrid courses will incorporate research-based pedagogies and innovative technologies. Courses will be offered in both instructor-led and student-directed learning formats to study the differences in learning outcome, if any, between these two different approaches. This project will provide important information regarding optimal methods to deliver interdisciplinary cybersecurity curricula and how the education community can effectively broaden access to cybersecurity education beyond typical classroom courses. The project team will conduct outreach activities to ensure participation by underrepresented populations and will disseminate findings through workshops at relevant meetings of professional societies. 

This project is supported by a special initiative of the Secure and Trustworthy Cyberspace (SaTC) program to foster new, previously unexplored, collaborations between the fields of cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and education. The SaTC program aligns with the Federal Cybersecurity Research and Development Strategic Plan and the National Privacy Research Strategy to protect and preserve the growing social and economic benefits of cyber systems while ensuring security and privacy.

abstractText:
In response to the quick development and adoption of connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs), U.S. cities and states have recently started building CAV cyberinfrastructure. However, there is not an adequate supply of skilled research workforce in this field. A key obstacle to such workforce development is the lack of well-structured training programs for utilizing CAV cyberinfrastructure to enable and potentially transform fundamental CAV research. To address this issue, a project-oriented training program will be developed in this CyberTraining project to enable scientific research workforce development for CAV cyberinfrastructure. It is estimated that the adoption of CAVs would lead to nearly $800 billion in annual social and economic benefits by 2050, therefore, it is important for the nation to invest in CAV cyberinfrastructure research workforce training programs. The proposed training program targets students and early-stage researchers who are interested in CAVs, including participants with a broad diversity in academic level and in experience level with CAVs. It is expected that more than 100 trainees will participate every year in the training program, including researchers from various domains such as cyber-physical systems, edge computing, wireless networking, deep learning, computer vision, and big data. A longstanding collaboration with the trainees and/or their advisors will be built to ensure a broad adoption of CAV cyberinfrastructure by the research community to catalyze major research advances. The long-term goal of this project is to develop a first of its kind open CAV cyberinfrastructure, an integrated training and research hub, to accelerate research and education in CAVs.

The goal of this project is to develop a collaborative and integrated training program to enable scientific research work force development for Connected and Autonomous Vehicle CyberInfrastructure (CAV-CI) and foster broad adoption of CAV-CI to advance fundamental CAV related research. To achieve these goals, the project will leverage existing partnerships with relevant stakeholders to create tailored, high-impact, engaging, collaborative, and integrated training modules for CAV-CI research workforce development. With the aim of enhancing trainees design and implementation capabilities, problem-solving skills, and critical thinking ability, the proposed training program will result in: (1) a project-oriented short course plus long-term coaching and support, (2) hands-on training modules on the perception, network, and application layers in CAV-CI, (3) an annual research workshop that disseminates research results and receives feedback on the training  program from the research and industrial communities, and (4) research projects for students supported through NSF's Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU)program and capstone projects for senior undergraduates. During the training workshops, project-oriented training will be offered to actively engage trainees in learning and solving real-world problems. Three sample research projects will be designed, allowing trainees to develop complete research skills, i.e., competency to solve authentic problems. Following every sample research project, with each having a strong practical relevance and meaningfulness, two versions of training modules will be developed to reach a broader trainee group: a fundamental training module for undergraduate students and community college educators, and a research-intensive training module for graduate students and postdocs. By taking either the fundamental or the research-intensive training modules, trainees will enhance their problem-solving skills, improve their creative and independent thinking ability, as well as gaining enthusiasm and confidence in conducting CAV-CI enabled research.  The CAV-CI education, research and training activities include specific goals to train individuals from underrepresented groups and the broader STEM workforce.

projectOutComesReport:
We developed a series of six training modules aimed at advancing the development of the scientific research workforce for Connected and Autonomous Vehicle Cyber Infrastructure (CAV-CI) and promoting the widespread adoption of CAV-CI to drive innovation in CAV technologies. These modules cover a wide range of critical topics, equipping students and educators with the necessary knowledge and skills to tackle challenges in the field. Module 1 introduces trainees to autonomous vehicle sensors and the basics of processing raw sensor data for cooperative perception. Module 2 delves into the complexities of achieving feature-map level cooperative perception, including techniques for generating and fusing feature maps from LiDAR data. In Module 3, trainees explore the architecture of vehicular edge computing systems and learn how to process data across different layers, from vehicles to the cloud. Module 4 builds on this foundation by guiding trainees to develop solutions for creating reliable and heterogeneous vehicular edge computing systems. Module 5 focuses on deep learning algorithms, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), for object detection in CAVs. Finally, Module 6 addresses advanced techniques for improving object detection accuracy, particularly for small and distant objects. Together, these modules provide a comprehensive foundation in CAV technologies, preparing trainees to tackle the evolving challenges in the field. In addition to these training modules, we launched a graduate-level course at UNT, Connected and Autonomous Vehicle Systems, designed to offer a deeper understanding of the key techniques needed for CAV research. This course, built on the concepts taught in the modules, methodically addresses the challenges of sensing, computing, and communication in autonomous vehicles. By offering a structured learning path, the course ensures that the next generation of researchers is well-equipped to contribute to the rapidly advancing field of CAVs.

To ensure the effective dissemination of the training modules, we organized a series of tailored sessions designed to prepare undergraduate students for research opportunities, particularly those funded by the NSF REU program and the University of North Texas' Undergraduate Research Fellowship. These sessions provided students with hands-on experience and foundational knowledge, enabling them to engage in meaningful research projects related to connected and autonomous vehicle (CAV) technologies. In addition, we hosted a special training session for community college professors, aimed at equipping them with the necessary tools to teach and mentor students in this rapidly evolving field. We also conducted a tutorial at the IEEE MetroCAD conference, which catered to both industry and academic researchers, and two more specialized workshops for a diverse group of researchers from industry research labs and universities, further promoting the adoption of CAV-CI technologies across various sectors. As a result of these efforts, over 70 undergraduate and graduate students, as well as more than 40 professors and industry professionals, received comprehensive training on CAV technologies. Many students who participated in these sessions are now pursuing careers as assistant professors, research scientists, and experts in various research labs and academic institutions. Their contributions to the research community have been substantial, resulting in the publication of over 30 peer-reviewed journal and conference papers, five Ph.D. dissertations, and one undergraduate thesis, further advancing the state of knowledge in CAV technologies.

abstractText:
Data formats and annotation standards vary widely for transcribed and translated linguistic data. This means the data cannot be readily mined for hypothesis testing and typological discovery. The University of North Texas will host a meeting of linguistic experts working with genetically closely related languages to explore consensus building on shared annotation standards for Interlinear Glossed Texts (IGT). IGT is a popular output of documentation projects and present language data with morpheme, word, and clause translation. This data format is a powerful way to discover and illustrate grammatical description. Three sessions at the conference will feature experts’ conversation on: 

Session 1: Standards and procedures for the creation of Interlinear Gloss Texts (IGT) 
Session 2: A generalized ontology for annotating linguistic concepts for related languages 
Session 3: Metadata for linguistic concepts in digital and legacy archival materials 

Expert recommendations of an advisory board and conference participants will be documented in a white paper. The white paper will focus on lessons learned including: the power of cross corpora comparison for grammatical analysis, reuse of archived data through improved metadata, and incorporating information of legacy data into current investigations for improved analysis and results. Recordings, presentations, and discussion will be archived at the University of North Texas Digital Library. Two graduate students will gain experience in academic professionalism. One of the graduate students will also gain knowledge of many aspects of grammar, language documentation, language annotation, and language archiving.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
